qs.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and foul-smelling stools. Serological testing reveals positive anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. If a duodenal biopsy is performed, which human leukocyte antigen genotype is most strongly associated with this condition?
qs.e: Coeliac disease is strongly linked to the HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8 alleles, which are present in the vast majority of affected patients. HLA-B27 is typically associated with seronegative spondyloarthropathies rather than gluten-sensitive enteropathy.

qs.q: How is persistent diarrhea distinguished from acute and chronic diarrhea based on duration?
qs.e: Persistent diarrhea is specifically defined as diarrhea that persists from 2 to 4 weeks. Acute diarrhea lasts less than 2 weeks, and chronic diarrhea lasts more than 4 weeks.

qs.q: In evaluating a patient with chronic diarrhea, stool analysis for ova and parasites is negative. What is the appropriate next diagnostic step according to the evaluation pathway?
qs.e: If the stool analysis for ova and parasites is negative in chronic diarrhea, the next step in the workup is to perform a stool fat test to evaluate for malabsorption. Infection must be ruled out first before checking for fat malabsorption.

qs.q: A toddler presents with chronic diarrhea, foul-smelling stools, abdominal bloating, and a history of drinking contaminated water during recent travel. What is the appropriate diagnostic approach?
o: Microscopic examination of stool for ova and parasites
Rectal biopsy to look specifically for ganglion cells
Stool culture to rule out common bacterial pathogens
Hydrogen breath test for carbohydrate malabsorption
qs.e: Microscopic examination of stool for ova and parasites, along with stool antigen tests, is used to diagnose parasitic infections like Giardia intestinalis. Stool culture is reserved for suspected bacterial pathogens presenting with fever and bloody stools.

qs.q: A patient with achlorhydria presents with severe chronic diarrhea and foul-smelling fatty stools. Which host factor directly increases the susceptibility to developing a Giardia lamblia infection?
o: Presence of blood group O phenotype
qs.e: Achlorhydria, or the absence of stomach acid, is a recognized risk factor that increases susceptibility to Giardia lamblia infection. Normal gastric acidity usually acts as a barrier against ingested cysts.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with chronic diarrhea. Which duration threshold defines chronic diarrhea according to clinical standards?
o: Duration exceeds four to six weeks
Duration lasts from two to four weeks
Duration lasts under two weeks time
Duration extends past three months total
qs.e: Chronic diarrhea is defined as symptoms lasting longer than 4-6 weeks. Diarrhea lasting less than 2 weeks is typically classified as acute and is usually due to infectious causes.

qs.q: A patient with chronic diarrhea is suspected of having carbohydrate malabsorption. Which laboratory finding supports this diagnosis?
o: Stool pH measuring less than six units
Decreased breath hydrogen gas production levels
Fecal osmotic gap less than fifty mOsm
Stool fat greater than six grams daily
qs.e: Carbohydrate malabsorption is characterized by a stool pH less than 6, a stool osmotic gap greater than 100, and increased breath hydrogen. Stool fat greater than 6g daily is indicative of fat malabsorption.

qs.q: How long must a decrease in fecal consistency persist to be classified as chronic diarrhea?
qs.e: Chronic diarrhea is defined as a decrease in fecal consistency lasting for 4 weeks or more, which requires a formal workup. Acute diarrhea lasts less than 2 weeks.

ai.title: Chronic Diarrhoea in Paediatrics
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Chronic diarrhoea (>4 weeks) in children is a diagnostic challenge in low‑resource settings. A systematic approach—history, exam, targeted tests—helps identify infectious, inflammatory, osmotic or malabsorptive causes and guide management.

sections.p: Chronic diarrhoea is loose stools >4 weeks, or >3 stools/day for >4 weeks. Diagnosis requires ruling out acute causes and confirming persistence.
Use the WHO malnutrition and dehydration scales; classify as mild, moderate or severe based on weight loss, dehydration signs and growth faltering.
In East Africa, infections dominate. Follow a hierarchy: infectious, inflammatory, malabsorptive, osmotic, medication‑related.

faq.q: What is the first test to order in a child with chronic diarrhoea in a low‑resource setting?
faq.a: Stool microscopy for parasites and bacterial culture, as these are common and inexpensive.

faq.q: How do you differentiate osmotic from secretory diarrhoea?
faq.a: Calculate fecal osmotic gap; a gap >200 mOsm/kg suggests osmotic, <200 mOsm/kg suggests secretory.

faq.q: Why is oral rehydration solution preferred over IV fluids in most cases?
faq.a: It corrects electrolytes, is inexpensive, can be given orally, and reduces hospital stay.

exam: What is the most likely cause of chronic diarrhoea in a 5‑year‑old boy from a rural East African village with weight loss and night‑time diarrhoea? — Consider parasitic infections (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Isospora) and malaria; order stool microscopy and malaria test.

A child presents with chronic diarrhoea and blood in stool. Which investigation would you order first and why? — Fecal calprotectin to rule out inflammatory bowel disease; if high, proceed to colonoscopy.
You suspect HIV enteropathy in a child with chronic diarrhoea. What is the next step in management? — Perform a rapid HIV test; if positive, start ART and consider prophylaxis.

A child has chronic diarrhoea but normal stool microscopy and cultures. What is the next diagnostic step? — Measure fecal fat to assess malabsorption; if positive, consider celiac disease or pancreatic insufficiency.
Why should you avoid giving antibiotics empirically in chronic diarrhoea? — It can worsen dysbiosis, cause resistance, and mask underlying causes.
A child with chronic diarrhoea is dehydrated. Which fluid should you give first? — Oral rehydration solution; if severe, start IV isotonic saline.
What is the key difference between osmotic and secretory diarrhoea on stool osmotic gap? — Osmotic gap >200 mOsm/kg indicates osmotic; <200 mOsm/kg indicates secretory.
When is surgical referral indicated in chronic diarrhoea? — Persistent bloody diarrhoea, failure to respond to medical therapy, or evidence of obstruction or perforation.
